newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Slow start to Liberia disarmament.
newsitem.headline: Slow start to Liberia disarmament.

text.p: Liberia's estimated 60,000 faction fighters began disarming on Friday but the process started slowly with civilians sceptical and fighters mistrustful of rivals.
General Victor Malu, head of a Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force, expressed satisfaction with the process, which is a condition for national elections next May.
"I'm satisfied with the way the exercise has begun and it is going to be exciting. I have no doubt in my mind about that," he told reporters in the capital Monrovia.
The U.N. Children's Fund has urged that child soldiers be given priority in the process, due to end on January 31.

Members of the former national army, which fought alongside ethnic Krahn factions in a flare-up in Monrovia in April and May, handed weapons to peacekeepers and U.N. military observers at Schiefflin barracks, 25 km (15 miles) from the capital.
In Kakata, 80 kim (50 miles) northeast on Monrovia, gunmen expressed concerns about handing over their weapons.
"We will wait for a little while to see that everyone is complying," said General Nice, a follower of Charles Taylor, the man who launched the war in December 1989.
"Our worry is what happens after disarmament? Are we going to see our enemies attacking us," Taylor's chief of staff General George Duwana added.
Freed American slaves set up Liberia in 1847. The war has killed well over 150,000 people. The Monrovia flare-up killed hundreds.
Disarmament is part of a peace deal brokered by West African heads of state in Nigeria in August. They have threatened sanctions against any warlord derailing it.
